content.text:
I've read the calendar's topbar, the board's drag code, the data layer and the local file mirror. Here's what the code already settles, so I won't ask about it:

- **Every file is already on the device.** The repo is mirrored into IndexedDB (`shared/store.js`, `allFiles(prefix)`), so search can run locally and offline, results can update on every keystroke, and nothing has to go to the GitHub API.
- **The magnifier is the zoom button today** (`calendar/ui.js:145`). Giving it to search means zoom needs a new icon, as you said.
- **Board drag is desktop-only by design** (`kanban.js:54`, it sets `draggable` only when not on a phone). Phones get ‹ › arrows on each card. HTML5 drag-and-drop doesn't fire on touch, so mobile drag means rewriting it with pointer events.
- **Moving one occurrence of a repeating entry already works**: `patchOccurrence` writes an override, which is what the board does now.
- **Calendar is the only app.** `spike/` is a test page.

**Question 1: what does "installed globally" mean for search?**

Since calendar is the only app, "global" can mean two things:

- **(A) A shared module.** Add `shared/search.js` for the search box, the live results and markdown-aware matching. Each app calls it with its own folder (`calendar/`) and a function that turns a result into a row it can open (for calendar, opening the entry popup). The main Mine screen gets no search.
- **(B) Option A, plus a search on the Mine home screen** that covers all of mine-data and hands each result to the app that owns it.

**I recommend A.** It matches "for the calendar app it shall only search the calendar folder", and with one app the home-screen search in B would only repeat the calendar's own. B can be added later without changing A.

Which one do you mean, or something else?

content.text:
**Question 2: what should "markdown-optimized" mean in practice?**

My proposal for matching:

- **Fields searched:** the frontmatter `title` counts most, then the body. For calendar, also the group's label and the participants. Other frontmatter keys are left out, so `stage: todo` doesn't turn up for "todo".
- **Body read as text, not syntax:** `**bold**`, `# headings`, `- [ ]` checkboxes and backticks are stripped before matching, and a link matches on its visible text, not its URL.
- **Query:** every word has to appear somewhere (AND), each word can match the start of a word (`dent` finds "dentist"), and case and accents are ignored (`cafe` finds "Café"). No fuzzy or typo matching.
- **Ranking:** title matches come first, then body-only matches. Within each group, the closest date to today goes first, upcoming before past.
- **Results:** one row per file, with the title, the date and a short snippet of the body around the match with the matched words highlighted.

Does this match what you meant, or did you have something else in mind, such as full fuzzy search or searching any frontmatter key?

Understood. The shared module then can't know anything about calendar fields, so I'm changing two things:

- **No calendar-only fields.** Group label and participants are out. Search covers the title and the body. Other frontmatter values I'd also search, but with body weight. The cost is that `todo` finds tasks in that stage, which is harmless since that text really is in the file.
- **The module only sees files, not entries.** It returns a path, title, date and snippet. The app decides what clicking a result does: calendar opens the entry popup, and a Zettelkasten would open the zettel.

**Question 3: where do the title and date come from? Is that a requirement or a fallback?**

Calendar files already have `title:` but store their date as `start:`, not `date:`. A hard rule of "frontmatter must have `title` and `date`" would mean renaming `start` in every calendar file or making an exception for it. It would also make a hand-written zettel with no frontmatter impossible to find.

I recommend a **fallback chain in the search** plus a **soft rule in the root REQUIREMENTS.md**:

- **title:** frontmatter `title`, else the first `# heading`, else the file name.
- **date:** frontmatter `date`, else `start`, else a `YYYY-MM-DD` in the path, else none. A file with no date ranks after the dated ones and shows no date.
- **The rule:** "Every markdown file should have a title and a date. Search reads them from `title` and `date`/`start`, falling back to the first heading and the path." This states the convention without making a file that breaks it disappear.

Shall I go with this, or do you want a strict requirement so the search can skip the fallbacks?

content.text:
Good idea. Each app says which keys mean what, and the module stays generic. My proposal for the call:

```js
openSearch({
  folder: 'calendar/',
  title:  'title',                  // key holding the title
  date:   'start',                  // key holding the date
  fields: ['group', 'participants'],// extra keys searched, at body weight
  open:   path => …                 // what clicking a result does
})
```

- **Keys left out fall back** to the first `# heading` / file name for the title and a date in the path for the date. A Zettelkasten can call it with just `{ folder, open }`.
- **Only keys the app lists are searched**, which drops my earlier "every frontmatter value" idea. `stage: todo` no longer matches unless the app asks for it.

**Question 4: which files in the folder count as documents?**

`calendar/` also holds `groups.md`, `settings.md` and override files. An override holds only the keys that differ, usually with no `title`. None of these should be results of their own.

I recommend this rule: **if the app names a `title` key, a file without it isn't a document.** That drops groups, settings and title-less overrides with no special cases. A repeating entry then shows up once, as its series file, and calendar's `open` opens its next occurrence from today, or the last one if the series has ended. The catch is that an override that rewrote one occurrence's body won't be found by words that appear only in that body. I think that's acceptable.

Would you rather have an explicit `skip` list or predicate instead, or does the title-key rule work?

content.text:
**Question 5: how the search popup behaves.**

My proposal:

- **Placement:** a centred popup like the day preview. The top row is the text input with the cursor already in it (the phone keyboard opens straight away) and the `x` rightmost. Results are listed below and scroll.
- **Live:** the list updates on every keystroke. With a few thousand small files in memory that's fast, so there's no debounce. The list is capped at 50 rows, with a "50+ matches, keep typing" line when there are more.
- **Empty input:** the list is empty.
- **Clicking a result** opens the entry popup over the search. Closing the entry brings you back to the search with the query and scroll position kept, so you can try the next result. The `x` or Escape on the search closes it.
- **Filter:** search ignores the calendar filter. When you're looking for something, a hidden group quietly dropping results would be confusing. The module stays simpler too, with no filter hook.

**Question 6: topbar layout and the zoom icon.**

Today the bar is `[board][zoom] ‹ period › [menu][home]`. On a phone the two sides form row 1 and `‹ period ›` is row 2. Search and filter add two buttons.

**Layout, three buttons a side so the phone's first row stays balanced:**
```
[board][zoom][search]   ‹ period ›   [filter][menu][home]
```
The filter's active-count badge moves from the hamburger to the filter button. The hamburger keeps just **settings** and **logs**, still as a two-row menu rather than a direct link, since two errands still need naming.

**Zoom icon.** The magnifier goes to search, and the board button already shows three columns. I recommend **the button shows its current state as text instead of an icon**: `D`, `W`, `M` or `Y` in a calendar view (rendered like the `24h` and `!` glyphs). On the board it shows a small icon of the current orientation: three bars side by side for horizontal, three stacked for vertical. That tells you where you are as well as where to tap, which no generic "view" icon does.

The alternative is a fixed **layers** icon (two stacked diamonds), the usual "change view" symbol, which looks the same in every mode.

Do you want the state-showing button or a fixed icon? And does the 3 + 3 layout work for you?

content.text:
**Question 7: dragging the topbar to the top or bottom.**

The bar is almost all buttons, so a plain drag would fight with taps. Some decisions:

- **How it's grabbed:** press and hold anywhere on the bar for about 400 ms, buttons included. The bar lifts, follows your finger or mouse, and on release snaps to whichever half of the screen it's in. A tap or a short press stays a tap. The other option is a small grip handle, but there's no free room for one on the phone's first row.
- **Scope:** one position for the whole calendar app, month and board alike, remembered per device the way the board orientation is (`setKV`).
- **What follows it:** when the bar is at the bottom, the sync line moves to the top so they don't stack. The popups anchored to bar buttons (zoom, picker, filter, menu) open upward. On a phone at the bottom the rows swap order, so `‹ period ›` sits on the upper row and the icons are nearest the thumb. The bar also respects the home-indicator safe area.

**A simpler option:** a "toolbar: top / bottom" row in settings would do the same thing with none of the gesture code. Since you asked for drag-and-drop I'd build the press-and-hold drag, but say if a settings row is good enough.

Should I go with press-and-hold drag, the settings row, or both?

Horizontal on a phone shows one column at a time, so the drop target is usually off screen. My proposal:

- **One drag implementation for every device.** Pointer events replace the current HTML5 drag on desktop too, because HTML5 drag doesn't fire on touch. The same small helper drives the board, the calendar grids and the topbar.
- **Pick up with press-and-hold (~400 ms)**, like the topbar, so a normal swipe still scrolls the column. The card lifts and follows your finger. On a desktop with a mouse, pick-up happens after a few pixels of movement with no hold.
- **While a card is held on the phone's horizontal board, three drop zones appear** in a strip over the column header, `todo · doing · done` in their stage colours. You drop on one. That's a better fit than pushing against the screen edge to page the columns, which is fiddly and easy to trigger by accident. Stacked (vertical) needs no strip: you drop on the stage itself, and the board scrolls when you hold near the top or bottom edge.
- **The ‹ › arrows on phone cards are removed.** They exist only because there was nothing to drag onto (`kanban.js:105`), and keeping them means two ways to do one thing, right next to the header's look-alike pager. Tapping a card still opens it, and the popup can still change the stage.

Do you agree with the drop strip, and with removing the card arrows? Or would you rather keep the arrows as well?

content.text:
**Question 9: dragging entries between dates.**

- **Views:** month and week. The day view has only one day to drop on, and the year view draws coloured days rather than entries, so neither gets drag.
- **Pick-up:** the same press-and-hold as the board. On a phone a short press still opens the entry and a swipe still scrolls.
- **Target is a day.** In the week view the entry keeps its time even if you drop it at another height in the hour grid; only the column (the day) counts, as you said. Timed entries keep their wall-clock time in the configured zone, so a 09:00 stays 09:00 across a DST change.
- **Multi-day:** whichever day of the span you grabbed, the day you release on becomes the new start, and the end moves by the same number of days.
- **Repeating entries:** dragging moves that one occurrence only, as an override, the same way the board moves one. There's no "move the whole series" option.
- **Tasks** move with their dates. If that moves one into another sprint, it changes boards, which is how sprints already work.
- **Only drawn lines can be dragged.** Entries hidden behind a month cell's `+3` can't, and neither can entries in the day preview.

Anything to change, especially week view keeping the time, or repeating entries moving one occurrence only?

I'd make **one commit per feature**, in this order: search, topbar (filter, search, zoom button), shared drag helper with board drag, entry drag, docking bar. Each commit carries its own doc and test changes. Nothing gets pushed unless you ask.

content.content:
and a card is read at the width a sentence is read at, not at a third of the screen. The pane
itself is full width in both, so it never changes shape when you switch between them.

In the top pane, three groups: the two view controls at the left, the period in the middle, the
two ways out at the right.

```
[board]    [zoom]     [‹]   [NOV/26]   [›]     [☰] [⌂]     a calendar view
[calendar] [zoom]     [‹]   [7]        [›]     [☰] [⌂]     the kanban
```

Everything in the pane is drawn at **twice the size** it was: this is the row reached for on
every visit, and it was the smallest thing on the screen.

**On a phone the pane is two rows**, each one filling the width:

```
[board]  [zoom]  [☰]   [⌂]         the four that go somewhere
[‹]     [ NOV/26 ]     [›]         the period, and the way to another
```

Five controls across one line left the period label — the one thing in the pane you read rather
than aim at — no wider than the buttons beside it, and the arrows that step it had to be dropped
to make even that fit. A second row buys back both. **The four controls that go somewhere share
the first row equally**; the period takes the second, where **the two arrows are equal in size
and the label between them is larger**, because the label carries a date to be read and an arrow
carries only a direction. The pane still fits a 320 px viewport, and neither row drops a control
or lets one wrap away.

- **Leftmost, the view switch and the zoom.** One slot always holds the way to the other kind
  of view: a board icon in a calendar view, and on the board a calendar icon, which returns to
  the month view. The board is not a zoom step, which is why it has a slot of its own rather
  than a place in the zoom's list. Beside it the **zoom**, drawn as a magnifier — described
  below.
- **Centred, the period.** Left/right buttons, with the period label between them, to move to
  the previous/next day, week, month, year or sprint, depending on the current view. The label
  is short, because the pane has to fit a phone:

  | view | label |
  | --- | --- |
  | day | `FR 20/NOV` |
  | week | `W47/NOV` |
  | month | `NOV/26` |
  | year | `2026` |
  | kanban | `7` — the sprint number alone |

  The month name is the device locale's three-letter abbreviation, upper-cased, so a German
  phone reads `OKT/26`: short beats English. The week label always carries its ISO week number,
  whether or not *show calendar weeks* is on — that setting governs the month view's gutter and
  nothing else. A week spanning two months takes the month its **fourth** day is in, which is
  the rule the gutter already uses, so label and gutter can never disagree.

  **Clicking the label opens the picker**, and that is the only thing it does — in every view
  and on a phone as much as on a desktop. **There is no caret `▾`.** The caret existed only
  because the label's own tap was taken by the zoom; the zoom is a button of its own now, so the
  label is free to be the one thing it was always read as — the period, pressed to pick another.
  This is also what the board has always done, so the two kinds of view no longer differ in what
  their label means. The label carries no glyph saying it is pressable: it takes a hover and a
  press background, as the year view's month caption does.

  The picker shows a month at a time, with its name top left and left/right arrows top right.
  Clicking the month name switches to a year grid of 9 years ending with the current one, whose
  arrows page by 9 years. Today is highlighted in it, and tapping it is how you get back to today
  — there is no jump-to-today button in the pane. In the kanban the picker picks a sprint: its
  rows read `Sprint 7 · 19 Jan – 1 Feb`, and the row holding today reads
  `current · 19 Jan – 1 Feb` on a brighter background in dark mode, a darker one in light.

  **The two arrows stand well clear of the label.** On a desktop the gap either side of it is
  about half an arrow — three controls crammed together read as one control, and this is the
  group the pane is used through. On a phone the second row keeps its tight gap, because there
  the arrows are flexible halves and every millimetre of gap is taken off a thumb's target.

  **On a phone the `‹` `›` are on the second row, drawn at the size of the first row's icons.**
  They were larger than everything above them, which made the row that steps the period louder
  than the four that leave it. And **there is no swipe anywhere in the calendar**: the label was
  swiped only because the arrows were not there to press; now that they have a row of their own
  they are, and a gesture doing what a visible button does is the same second mechanism this
  document refuses a card on a desktop. So no sideways gesture does anything, in any view, and
  nothing ever has to be told apart from a card drag on the board or from a scroll in a grid.
- **Rightmost, the two ways out.** A **hamburger** button that names its three errands — `filter`,
  `settings` and `logs` — and opens whichever is tapped, and a home icon back to the Mine tile
  screen. A house rather than an arrow, because a third arrow beside the two that step through
  periods reads as another way to move inside the calendar.

### The zoom

A magnifier beside the view switch, opening a short list under itself. **It offers what the view
it was opened in can do, and nothing else:**

| view | the list |
| --- | --- |
| day, week, month, year | `day` · `week` · `month` · `year` |
| kanban | `vertical` · `horizontal` |

The current one is marked. In a calendar view this is the whole of the zoom: it replaces the
label's cycle, which walked year → month → week → day → year and so asked for up to three taps
to reach the view you wanted and gave you no way to see which one you were in without reading
the label. A list of four names you point at is one tap and says both. There is still no `-` and
no `+` in the pane, and no `D` `W` `M` `Y` `K` row across it either — the four names are in a
popup, not spread along the row the period lives on.

On the board the same button carries the board's own one choice, its **orientation**, because a
board has no period to zoom. The two never appear together: a calendar view cannot be stacked
and a board cannot be a week.

**The orientation is remembered per device** and starts at `horizontal`. It is a preference
about this screen, like *confirm discard*, so it is kept where the rest of them are and has a
row in neither the panel nor the repo. The calendar's own zoom is **not** remembered: the app
opens on the month, on today, on the current sprint, as it always has — which view you were last
in is where you were, not what you prefer.

Cards are not reordered by hand; their order comes from importance and start — the important ones
first, each block by start date.

## The filter, the settings and the logs

**One button, three errands, named before any opens.** The hamburger opens a short dropdown
reading `filter`, `settings` and `logs`, and opens none of them; a second tap opens the one that
was meant. One button still covers them all, so the pane stays at four controls and the phone's
first row does not gain a fifth — but the button no longer decides which of them you came for.

They were one panel for a while, under a heading each. A heading is a weak way to separate a thing
you open daily from a thing you open twice, and it cost the filter the room to show its groups:
the list had to be folded away or it pushed the nine settings rows below the fold. Naming the two
and opening them apart costs one tap and buys each of them its own shape.

**The filter is a dropdown off the hamburger.** It is the half you open often — a group hidden
this afternoon, the board narrowed to what is important — and the view it narrows has to stay in
sight while it is narrowed, which a centred card over the middle of the screen cannot do.

**The settings are a centred panel**, titled `Settings`, whose top right has an `x` to close.
They are the nine rows that change once, so they may take the middle of the screen.

**The logs are a centred panel too**, titled `Logs`, and they are the answer to a sync line that
says something unexpected. The line `14 change(s) pending` used to be the whole of what the app
would say about a queue that could not drain: the reason was written to that same line by
whichever push failed and overwritten by the next focus, so a browser could sit on a count it
could neither explain nor clear. The panel holds three things —

- **the state**, with `push now` and `discard all` beside it;
- **the last attempt**: whether it was a push or a pull, what it failed with, how many times in a
  row, and since when;
- **what is waiting**: one line per queued change — `put` or `del`, its path, and how long it has
  been there.

`push now` is the same drain the app runs on open and on focus, so the panel adds no second way
to sync. `discard all` is the one control in Mine that can lose work, so it confirms through the
browser's own prompt, the way *forget this device* does on the tile screen, rather than through
the calendar's discard prompt — whose **don't ask again** would switch this guard off along with
the one it belongs to. Discarding also forgets the local copy of every path it held and drops the
ETag, so the next pull restores exactly what GitHub holds; forgetting the queue alone would leave
text in the mirror that no later pull would ever reconcile.

**The sync line is a button.** It is what you are looking at when you want to know why it says
what it says, and reaching the panel through the hamburger only helps once you know the panel is
there.

| overlay | holds |
| --- | --- |
| Filter (a dropdown) | a **Category** row, a **Stage** row and **important only**; on the board also an **assignee** |
| Settings (a centred panel) | the nine rows below |
| Logs (a centred panel) | the last sync attempt, the changes still queued, `push now`, `discard all` |

**The stages and importance narrow every view, not only the board.** The stage list holds a
checkbox per stage — `Todo`, `Doing`, `Done`, each with its colour. A month with the done ones out of it is as much a thing to want as a board of them.

A stage switched off hides **tasks** and nothing else: an event has no stage to be judged by.
`important only` hides whatever is not marked, **events included**, because that is what the
words say and a month of what matters is the thing worth having. Both are remembered per device,
like the groups: a filter that empties a month is one you want to find still on after a reload —
and the hamburger says it is.

**A filter that is on says so on the hamburger**: a small count at its top right, in a circle.
It counts **one per kind of narrowing** — the groups, the stages, importance, the assignee — so
it never passes four. One per switched-off thing would read `16` in a repo with twenty groups
and fifteen hidden, which is a true number nobody can act on; `3` says there are three things to
here: it is picked in the zoom, where it is read as a view control rather than as a setting.
Theme and date format apply to all of Mine, not the calendar alone, and the main app's settings
shows the same two rows.

## On a phone

The views above describe the desktop. The same screens adapt:

- The top pane is **two rows**: `[board] [zoom] [☰] [⌂]` sharing the first equally, and
  `[‹] [NOV/26] [›]` filling the second, at twice their old size and at every phone width, 320
  px included. The two arrows are equal, **drawn at the size of the icons on the row above**, and
  the label between them is larger than either and opens the picker. Nothing is swiped.
- A month cell shows at most two entry lines, then `+N`; a line carries the title alone, with no
  time prefix and no done-rectangle, clipped at the cell's edge. A year cell stays a coloured
  day.
- Tapping a day in the month or year view opens that day's entries as a centred card, each one

| view | the list |
| --- | --- |
| day, week, month, year | `day` · `week` · `month` · `year` |
| kanban | `vertical` · `horizontal` |

The current one is marked. In a calendar view this is the whole of the zoom: it replaces the
label's cycle, which walked year → month → week → day → year and so asked for up to three taps
to reach the view you wanted and gave you no way to see which one you were in without reading
the label. A list of four names you point at is one tap and says both. There is still no `-` and
no `+` in the pane, and no `D` `W` `M` `Y` `K` row across it either — the four names are in a
popup, not spread along the row the period lives on.

On the board the same button carries the board's own one choice, its **orientation**, because a
board has no period to zoom. The two never appear together: a calendar view cannot be stacked
and a board cannot be a week.

**The orientation is remembered per device** and starts at `horizontal`. It is a preference
about this screen, like *confirm discard*, so it is kept where the rest of them are and has a
row in neither the panel nor the repo. The calendar's own zoom is **not** remembered: the app
opens on the month, on today, on the current sprint, as it always has — which view you were last
in is where you were, not what you prefer.

Cards are not reordered by hand; their order comes from importance and start — the important ones
first, each block by start date.

## The filter, the settings and the logs

**One button, three errands, named before any opens.** The hamburger opens a short dropdown
reading `filter`, `settings` and `logs`, and opens none of them; a second tap opens the one that
was meant. One button still covers them all, so the pane stays at four controls and the phone's
first row does not gain a fifth — but the button no longer decides which of them you came for.

They were one panel for a while, under a heading each. A heading is a weak way to separate a thing
you open daily from a thing you open twice, and it cost the filter the room to show its groups:
the list had to be folded away or it pushed the nine settings rows below the fold. Naming the two
and opening them apart costs one tap and buys each of them its own shape.

**The filter is a dropdown off the hamburger.** It is the half you open often — a group hidden
this afternoon, the board narrowed to what is important — and the view it narrows has to stay in
sight while it is narrowed, which a centred card over the middle of the screen cannot do.

**The settings are a centred panel**, titled `Settings`, whose top right has an `x` to close.
They are the nine rows that change once, so they may take the middle of the screen.

**The logs are a centred panel too**, titled `Logs`, and they are the answer to a sync line that
says something unexpected. The line `14 change(s) pending` used to be the whole of what the app
would say about a queue that could not drain: the reason was written to that same line by
whichever push failed and overwritten by the next focus, so a browser could sit on a count it
could neither explain nor clear. The panel holds three things —

- **the state**, with `push now` and `discard all` beside it;
- **the last attempt**: whether it was a push or a pull, what it failed with, how many times in a
  row, and since when;
- **what is waiting**: one line per queued change — `put` or `del`, its path, and how long it has
  been there.

`push now` is the same drain the app runs on open and on focus, so the panel adds no second way
to sync. `discard all` is the one control in Mine that can lose work, so it confirms through the
browser's own prompt, the way *forget this device* does on the tile screen, rather than through
the calendar's discard prompt — whose **don't ask again** would switch this guard off along with
the one it belongs to. Discarding also forgets the local copy of every path it held and drops the
ETag, so the next pull restores exactly what GitHub holds; forgetting the queue alone would leave
text in the mirror that no later pull would ever reconcile.

**The sync line is a button.** It is what you are looking at when you want to know why it says
what it says, and reaching the panel through the hamburger only helps once you know the panel is
there.

| overlay | holds |
| --- | --- |
| Filter (a dropdown) | a **Category** row, a **Stage** row and **important only**; on the board also an **assignee** |
| Settings (a centred panel) | the nine rows below |
| Logs (a centred panel) | the last sync attempt, the changes still queued, `push now`, `discard all` |

**The stages and importance narrow every view, not only the board.** The stage list holds a
checkbox per stage — `Todo`, `Doing`, `Done`, each with its colour. A month with the done ones out of it is as much a thing to want as a board of them.

A stage switched off hides **tasks** and nothing else: an event has no stage to be judged by.
`important only` hides whatever is not marked, **events included**, because that is what the
words say and a month of what matters is the thing worth having. Both are remembered per device,
like the groups: a filter that empties a month is one you want to find still on after a reload —
and the hamburger says it is.

**A filter that is on says so on the hamburger**: a small count at its top right, in a circle.
It counts **one per kind of narrowing** — the groups, the stages, importance, the assignee — so
it never passes four. One per switched-off thing would read `16` in a repo with twenty groups
and fifteen hidden, which is a true number nobody can act on; `3` says there are three things to
here: it is picked in the zoom, where it is read as a view control rather than as a setting.
Theme and date format apply to all of Mine, not the calendar alone, and the main app's settings
shows the same two rows.

## On a phone

The views above describe the desktop. The same screens adapt:

- The top pane is **two rows**: `[board] [zoom] [☰] [⌂]` sharing the first equally, and
  `[‹] [NOV/26] [›]` filling the second, at twice their old size and at every phone width, 320
  px included. The two arrows are equal, **drawn at the size of the icons on the row above**, and
  the label between them is larger than either and opens the picker. Nothing is swiped.
- A month cell shows at most two entry lines, then `+N`; a line carries the title alone, with no
  time prefix and no done-rectangle, clipped at the cell's edge. A year cell stays a coloured
  day.
- Tapping a day in the month or year view opens that day's entries as a centred card, each one

content.content:
## Markdown bodies

Every app keeps its text as markdown, so every app has to show it. **One renderer, in `shared/`,
used by all of them** — the calendar's details body today, a zettelkasten note and a diary entry
next. Two renderers would drift, and a note that looked right in one app and wrong in the next
would be the plainest possible sign that these files are not as portable as the whole idea claims.

It is **deliberately small**, and covers what a personal note actually holds: paragraphs, `#` to
`###` headings, bullet and numbered lists, `- [ ]` and `- [x]` checkboxes, **bold**, *italic*,
`code`, and links. No tables, no blockquotes, no fenced code blocks and no images — each of them
is more code to own for something an agenda or a diary page rarely carries, and the app that first
genuinely needs one can add it then.

A checkbox is **rendered, not operated**: `- [x]` draws a ticked box, and ticking it is an edit of
the text like any other. A body is read far more often than its checklist is advanced, and a
tappable box would have to write a file from a screen whose whole point is that it writes nothing.

**It builds nodes, never HTML.** The renderer makes DOM elements and sets text, so nothing in a
body can turn into markup: a body carrying a `<script>` tag shows that tag as text. This is the
threat the CSP exists for — injected script on our own origin — and a data file in your own repo
is the likeliest thing to carry a stray angle bracket. A link is rendered only for `http`, `https`
and `mailto`; anything else stays text, so a `javascript:` URL is never something to press. Links
open in a new tab, because leaving the app would lose the view you were in.

It is hand-written rather than vendored. It is small enough to be, and the dependency table in
[TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) asks of everything in it what would be
wrong with hand-rolling it — for this, nothing.

## Using it

- Changes appear instantly and are queued for GitHub in the background.
- A sync indicator shows: in sync / pending / error. It is also a button: pressing it opens the
  calendar's `logs`, which says what the last attempt did and what is still waiting.
- Offline, the queue is kept and sent when you are back online or reopen the app. **Every open
  and every window focus retries it**, whatever went wrong last time, because a queue nothing
  retries is a queue that never empties — a browser left reporting a count it can neither
  explain nor clear.
- Editing the same entry on two devices never loses either version: the other device's version
  keeps the file, yours is kept beside it and flagged, and the sync indicator tells you there is
  something to review. Nothing is discarded and nothing is silently overwritten — but the app
  does not interrupt you to ask which to keep, because by then you are somewhere else.
- Everything works offline, including dates and search, because the app keeps a full local copy.

python3 - <<'EOF'
p='REQUIREMENTS.md'; s=open(p).read()
a="## Using it\n"
b="""## Search

Every app gets the same search, **in `shared/`, over that app's own folder**: the calendar's
magnifier searches `calendar/` and nothing else, and a zettelkasten's would search its own. It
runs on the device's full copy of the repo, so it works offline and **lists as you type**.

It is **one search for every app, so it knows no app's format.** Each app says when it calls it
which folder is its own, which frontmatter key holds the title and which the date, which further
keys are worth searching, and what opening a result does. Every markdown file in Mine should have
a **title** and a **date**; where an app names no key for one, the search falls back — the title
to the first `#` heading and then the file name, the date to a `YYYY-MM-DD` in the path — so a
hand-written note with no frontmatter at all is still found. Where an app *does* name its title
key, a file without that key is not a document: that is how a folder's own settings files stay
out of the results.

What is matched:

- **The body as text, not as markdown.** Emphasis, heading marks, list and checkbox markers and
  backticks are dropped before matching, and a link matches on its words rather than its URL.
- **Every word of the query**, each one anywhere in the title, the body or a named key, and each
  one **at the start of a word**: `dent` finds "dentist", `entist` finds nothing. Case and accents
  are ignored, so `cafe` finds "Café". There is no fuzzy or typo matching.
- **Titles first**: a file whose title holds every word is listed before one where the body had
  to help. Within each, the nearest date to today first, what is coming before what has been,
  and an undated file last.

A result is a row with the title, the date and a line of the body around the first match, the
matched words marked. The list stops at 50 and says there are more; an empty query lists nothing.
It hangs from the top of the screen rather than being centred, because the list grows as you
type and a centred box would move its own input on every keystroke — and on a phone the keyboard
covers the lower half anyway.

## Using it
"""
assert s.count(a)==1; s=s.replace(a,b); open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
grep -n "shared/" TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md | head -20

content.content:
IndexedDB — that is the whole mechanism behind "enter the token once".

```
/index.html /manifest.json /sw.js
/style.css  the shared base      /home.css  the tile screen's own
/shared/  apps.js  store.js  github.js  md.js  markdown.js  prefs.js
          ui.js  sync.js  vendor/
/calendar/  index.html  app.js  data.js  ui.js  views.js  kanban.js  popup.js  settings.js
            style.css  icon.svg  sample/
/test/    run.sh  unit.mjs  serve.py  cdp.mjs  check-mine.mjs  check-calendar.mjs
```

No build step: no bundler, no CI, no node_modules. `git push` deploys, every page opens from
disk, all paths relative so the `/mine/` prefix needs no config.

The checks in `test/` hold to the same rule: `run.sh` drives a headless Chromium over the
DevTools protocol with nothing installed, and what it covers — and the two mistakes that make
it lie to you — are in [TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md](TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md). One browser suite per app,
`check-<slug>.mjs`, discovered by `run.sh` rather than listed in it, over the harness in
`cdp.mjs`.

`shared/ui.js` is the chrome every app builds its screens out of: the DOM helpers, the icon set,
the three overlay mechanisms and the settings row. `shared/sync.js` is the sync line and the logs
panel. Both exist because both apps had their own copy: the drain-then-pull sequence was written
twice, the icon set and the overlays sat in `calendar/ui.js`, and the logs panel - which reports
on a queue shared by every app - was reachable only from the calendar.

Two couplings were cut to get them out of the calendar. `closePops()` took its list of overlays
from a literal naming the calendar's; it now takes it from `registerPops()`, which an app calls
once at boot, and the `aria-expanded` it resets is tracked by `openPop()` rather than named. The
icon set is shared for the verbs and the two conventions REQUIREMENTS.md states for all of Mine -
a green disk saves, a red trashcan deletes - and an app merges its own subjects in with
`addIcons()`; a second app drawing its own trashcan is how those conventions would quietly stop
being conventions.

`shared/apps.js` exports the app list and is imported by the tile screen, `sw.js` and
`github.js`, so adding an app means editing one array, and its `files` are what the worker
precaches. The list is
written by hand on purpose: `install` uses `cache.addAll`, which rejects as a whole if any URL
404s, so a wrong entry fails loudly at install. A *missing* one fails silently, which is how
`shared/markdown.js` stayed out of the shell while `popup.js` imported it — an app installed and
taken offline before an entry was ever opened could not draw a details body.

## Adding an app

Everything shared is in place, so an app is its folder plus two one-line registrations.

1. **`/<slug>/`** with `index.html`, `icon.svg`, your modules, and `style.css` if it needs one.
   Also `REQUIREMENTS.md`, `TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md` and `sample/`, which is the convention
   [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md) states for every app.
2. **The head of `index.html`** carries the same CSP, viewport and theme-color as the others,
holds. Forgetting the queue alone would leave unpushable text in the mirror filed under the blob
SHA it was based on, which every later pull would compare as equal and skip forever.

## Service worker

Registered `{type: 'module'}` so it can import `shared/apps.js`. A version constant names the
cache; install precaches the shell. Same-origin requests are cache-then-revalidate.

Requests to `api.github.com` **bypass the worker entirely** — caching an API response would hand
back a stale ETag and silently break sync.

A new worker waits; the UI offers "Update ready — reload" and `skipWaiting()` runs only on tap —
of that banner, or of **Reload app** in Mine's settings, which calls `registration.update()` first.

**The offer is gated on the version, not on a worker waiting.** The worker answers a `version`
message over a `MessageChannel` port with its `VERSION` constant, and the page compares the
waiting worker's answer with the active one's; equal answers mean no banner. A worker that is
byte-identical to the running one can sit in `waiting` indefinitely, and `reg.waiting` alone as
import { APPS } from './shared/apps.js';

content.content:
- **A stacked stage keeps its header**: the coloured name and the `+`, as before.
- **The phone's `‹` `›` pager is horizontal's alone.** It exists because exactly one column is
  on screen and it is the only way to see another; stacked, all three are already there, so
  there is nothing to page and the header carries neither arrow. The rule that **exactly one
  column is visible** likewise describes horizontal on a phone and says nothing about vertical.
- **A card keeps its own `<` `>` on a phone in both**, because a phone has nothing to drag onto,
  and **a desktop card is dragged between stages in both**, because a stacked stage is as good a
  drop target as a column.
- Vertical is not a phone layout: it is offered at every width, since a desktop board can be as
  lopsided as a phone's.

A card shows:

- a top row with the title, and a `!` in front of it when the task is important. **No pen and no
  trashcan.** The pen said what clicking the card already does — and there is no pen anywhere in
  the calendar now. The trashcan put the one irreversible action on the board, a thumb's width
  from the title you were aiming at. **On a
  phone the row also carries `<` `>`** to move the card to the previous or next stage — `<`
  disabled in todo, `>` disabled in done. **On a desktop it does not**: all three columns are

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Serves the working tree for the browser checks, plus one synthetic route per app.

/__fixture/<app>.json is what test/check-<app>.mjs seeds the local mirror with. It is generated
rather than committed as markdown so that it always lands in the month the checks run in - a
fixture pinned to April would leave the month view empty and the checks green.

A new app adds a function here and names it in FIXTURES. An app with no data of its own - the
tile screen - takes the empty one, which still gets it a config and a mirror to open against.
"""
import http.server, json, os, sys
from datetime import date

REPO = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
PORT = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 8787

# Weekday offsets within the month, so there is always a Saturday task, a day with more entries
# than a phone cell shows, all-day items, and the long titles that used to blow the grid open.
#
# A row may carry a sixth item: extra frontmatter lines - `important: true` for the importance
# checks, a recurrence rule for the repeating ones, an `end:` for the multi-day ones. `{+n}` in
# one of those is the start day plus n, written out, so a span lands in the month being checked.
# An explicit `end:` replaces the one a timed row is given automatically.
ROWS = [
    (1,  "09:00", "Sprint planning",                  "work",   "event"),
    (1,  "14:00", "Review the open pull requests",    "work",   "task",  "todo",
     ["important: true"]),
    (2,  None,    "Dentist",                          "health", "event"),
    (3,  "08:30", "Standup",                          "work",   "event"),
    (3,  "11:00", "Write the quarterly board report", "work",   "task",  "doing"),
    (3,  "17:00", "Gym",                              "health", "event"),
    (5,  "13:00", "Deploy the release",               "work",   "task",  "todo"),
    (3,  None,    "Water the plants",                 "home",   "task",  "todo",
     ['recurrence: "FREQ=WEEKLY"']),
    (6,  "10:00", "Fix the bathroom tap",             "home",   "task",  "todo"),

content.content:
trip is written `start: 2026-04-20`, `end: 2026-04-22`. This is a deliberate divergence from RFC
5545, where an all-day `DTEND` is exclusive: the file says what the popup asked for and what a
person reading the repo by hand would mean, and an `.ics` export adds the day back.

Groups switched off in the filter are not shown in any view.

### The day preview
explicitly edit it.

## Overrides

A recurring file states the rule only. Anything that happens to a *single* occurrence — ticked,
moved, retitled, cancelled — is an override file in the date tree carrying `series:` and
`recurrence-id:`, holding only the keys that differ. The rule file is never rewritten, and since
each override is a fresh path it cannot conflict, even when two devices do it offline.

`exdate:` covers a plain skip where there is nothing to record — what the popup's trashcan writes
when the scope pair says `this`. It takes any override file for that occurrence with it, in the
same commit: the expansion tests `exdate` *before* it looks an override up, so a file left behind
would be read by nothing and shown nowhere.

## Rendering a range

1. Collect dated entries whose `start` falls in the range.
2. Expand every rule in `recurring/` over the range; drop dates in `exdate`, add `rdate`.
3. Replace an occurrence with the override matching `series` + `recurrence-id`; an override

### Moving an entry to another day

**In the month and the week, an entry is dragged onto another day.** A mouse picks it up by
moving it a few pixels; a finger by holding still on it for a moment, so a grid still scrolls
under a finger that only means to scroll — the same press-and-drag the board's cards use. The
day under it is marked, releasing moves the entry there, and the drop never also opens the entry
or the day preview. The day view has only one day to drop on and the year view draws coloured
days rather than entries, so neither has it. Only what is drawn can be picked up: an entry hidden
behind a month cell's `+3`, or listed in the day preview, is moved from its popup.

  Thursday, read in the configured zone, so it is still 09:00 across a DST change. In the week the
  target is the day's column and only that: dropped lower or higher in the hour grid, the entry
  keeps its time.

  new start**, and its end moves by the same number of days: a three-day trip held by its middle
  day and dropped on a Friday runs Friday to Sunday.
- **A repeating entry moves this one occurrence**, as an override — the same thing the board does
  when it moves one. There is no "move the whole series" by dragging; that is the popup's.
- **A task's sprint follows its date**, as it always has: a task dragged out of its sprint's
  range is on the next board.

### The day preview"""
assert a in s; s=s.replace(a,b); open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
